subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 13 periods = 520 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 8h 40min

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (lace around tablecloth), section 6.1 p.131
textbook_items_in_class.description: Akshi wants to put lace all around a rectangular tablecloth 3 m long and 2 m wide; find the length of lace required using P = 2 × (l + b) = 10 m.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Usha runs three rounds), section 6.1 p.131
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the total distance Usha travels if she takes three rounds of a square park of side 75 m; perimeter = 300 m, total distance = 900 m.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1a, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find missing length of a rectangle whose perimeter is 14 cm and breadth is 2 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1b, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the side length of a square whose perimeter is 20 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1c, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find missing breadth of a rectangle whose perimeter is 12 m and length is 3 m.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 6.1 p.132
homework.description: Find the third side of a triangle with perimeter 55 cm and two sides 20 cm and 14 cm.

time_bands.activity: Open with a quick physical walk around the classroom boundary — students count paces and notice they are adding all four sides. Link this concrete action to the definition: perimeter as total boundary length. Introduce the three formulas (rectangle, square, triangle) through the pattern students name aloud.

Walk through Example (lace around tablecloth), section 6.1 p.131 ("Akshi wants to put lace all around a rectangular tablecloth....") and Example (Usha runs three rounds), section 6.1 p.131 ("Find the total distance Usha travels if she takes three rounds...."), emphasising how opposite-side equality collapses the four-sided sum to 2 × (l + b) for rectangles and to 4 × s for squares.

Students work independently on Figure it Out Q1a, section 6.1 p.132 ("Find missing length of a rectangle whose perimeter is 14 cm...."), Figure it Out Q1b, section 6.1 p.132 ("Find the side length of a square whose perimeter is 20 cm."), and Figure it Out Q1c, section 6.1 p.132 ("Find missing breadth of a rectangle whose perimeter is 12 m...."). Invite students to say the formula aloud in their own words before computing.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is students adding only two sides (one length and one breadth) instead of applying 2 × (l + b), treating the rectangle as if only two sides need fencing. Watch for this during independent practice and ask students to count sides on their sketch before computing. Self-study pointer: Example (Usha runs three rounds), section 6.1 p.131, provides a further model for multi-round distance calculations.

periods.activity_title: Perimeter as Sum: Inverse Problems and Regular Polygons

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: A wire bent into a 5 cm × 3 cm rectangle is straightened and re-bent into a square; find the side length of the square.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5a, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: A 36 cm string is formed into a square; find the side length.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5b, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: A 36 cm string is formed into an equilateral triangle; find the side length.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5c, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: A 36 cm string is formed into a regular hexagon; find the side length.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 6.1 p.132
homework.description: Find the cost of fencing a rectangular park 150 m × 120 m at ₹40 per metre.

time_bands.activity: Revisit the perimeter formulas for rectangle, square, and triangle through three rapid-fire questions posed orally. Introduce the idea of a regular polygon: all sides equal and all angles equal. Derive the general rule perimeter = number of sides × side length from the square and equilateral-triangle patterns students already know.

Present Figure it Out Q2, section 6.1 p.132 ("A wire bent into a 5 cm × 3 cm rectangle is straightened and re-bent into a square....") as a pair-discussion task. Students must first find total wire length and then redistribute equally to four sides. Follow with Figure it Out Q5a, section 6.1 p.132 ("A 36 cm string is formed into a square....") and Figure it Out Q5b, section 6.1 p.132 ("A 36 cm string is formed into an equilateral triangle....").

Students tackle Figure it Out Q5c, section 6.1 p.132 ("A 36 cm string is formed into a regular hexagon...."), applying the general rule for regular polygons. Discuss as a class: why does the side length change as the number of sides changes, even though the total perimeter stays the same? Elicit the idea that the perimeter is fixed (the string length) while the side count varies.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse the formula direction — given perimeter, they multiply instead of divide to find side length. Emphasise that the formula is a two-way tool: it finds perimeter from sides, or sides from perimeter. Prompt them to write the formula first and then substitute before computing.
materials: A piece of string or thread (~40 cm) per pair

periods.activity_title: Perimeter in Action: Fencing, Tracks, and Dot Grids

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 6.1 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: A rectangular field 230 m × 160 m is fenced with 3 rounds of rope; find the total rope length needed.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.1 p.133
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the total distance Akshi covers in 5 rounds of the outer rectangular track (70 m × 40 m).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.1 p.133
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the total distance Toshi covers in 7 rounds of the inner rectangular track (60 m × 30 m); determine who ran further.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3a-f, section 6.1 p.133
textbook_items_in_class.description: Mark positions A, B, C on Akshi's track after 250 m, 500 m, 1000 m; mark X, Y, Z on Toshi's track after 250 m, 500 m, 1000 m.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (straight and diagonal units), section 6.1 p.135
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write the perimeters of four dot-grid figures in terms of straight (s) and diagonal (d) units.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out Q6, section 6.1 p.132 ("A rectangular field 230 m × 160 m is fenced with 3 rounds....") to practise scaling perimeter by number of rounds. Introduce the Matha Pachchi scenario: two concentric rectangular tracks of different dimensions. Students compute Akshi's total (Figure it Out Q1, section 6.1 p.133) and Toshi's total (Figure it Out Q2, section 6.1 p.133) and compare.

Students mark positions on Akshi's and Toshi's tracks using Figure it Out Q3a-f, section 6.1 p.133 ("Mark positions A, B, C on Akshi's track after 250 m, 500 m, 1000 m...."). This requires dividing cumulative distance by perimeter and locating the remainder along the track's sides — a positional reasoning challenge that builds on perimeter as a repeating distance.

Introduce Figure it Out (straight and diagonal units), section 6.1 p.135 ("Write the perimeters of four dot-grid figures in terms of straight (s) and diagonal (d) units."). Students measure dot-grid shapes, noting that diagonal segments are longer than straight ones. Discuss: why does a triangle that looks like it has perimeter 9 straight units actually have more?

periods.teacher_notes: The positional reasoning in the track question is new difficulty: students must find the remainder after whole laps and identify which side of the rectangle the runner is on. Encourage them to sketch the rectangle with side lengths labelled and walk along it mentally. A common slip is forgetting to account for the different perimeters of the inner and outer tracks when comparing distances.

periods.activity_title: Cutting, Rejoining, and Exploring Perimeter Extremes

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Estimate and Verify, section 6.1 p.134
textbook_items_in_class.description: Cut irregular paper shapes from a rough sheet; estimate total boundary length by eye, then measure with a scale or measuring tape to verify the perimeter. Also discuss whether the perimeter of a dot-grid triangle is 9 straight units or more than 9 units (diagonal vs. straight length).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Split and rejoin, section 6.1 p.136
textbook_items_in_class.description: Cut a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangular paper chit into two equal halves and rejoin in four different configurations (a–d); find the perimeter of each arrangement and then find an arrangement with perimeter 22 cm.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Split and rejoin Q b, section 6.1 p.136
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the perimeter of arrangement b (two 6 cm × 2 cm pieces joined in an L-shape with 2 cm overlap).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Split and rejoin Q c, section 6.1 p.136
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the perimeter of arrangement c (two pieces joined in a T-shape).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Split and rejoin Q d, section 6.1 p.136
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the perimeter of arrangement d (two pieces joined in a staircase configuration).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Split and rejoin (target 22 cm), section 6.1 p.136
textbook_items_in_class.description: Arrange the two 6 cm × 2 cm pieces to form a figure with perimeter exactly 22 cm.

time_bands.activity: Each student cuts an irregular shape from a rough sheet and estimates its perimeter by eye, then measures with a ruler. Use Estimate and Verify, section 6.1 p.134 ("Cut irregular paper shapes from a rough sheet; estimate total boundary length by eye....") to surface the insight that estimation requires attending to every side and that diagonal boundaries add more length than they appear to.

Students cut a 6 cm × 4 cm paper rectangle into two 6 cm × 2 cm halves and physically try four rejoining configurations from Split and rejoin, section 6.1 p.136 ("Cut a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangular paper chit into two equal halves...."). For each arrangement they sketch the shape, label sides, and compute perimeter for Split and rejoin Q b, section 6.1 p.136 ("Find the perimeter of arrangement b...."), Split and rejoin Q c, section 6.1 p.136, and Split and rejoin Q d, section 6.1 p.136.

Challenge: using Split and rejoin (target 22 cm), section 6.1 p.136 ("Arrange the two 6 cm × 2 cm pieces to form a figure with perimeter exactly 22 cm."), students find and record the configuration that achieves exactly 22 cm. Discuss why touching edges disappear from the boundary and how the number of shared edges controls the perimeter.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often assume that two shapes joined together always have more perimeter than either alone — the shared-edge phenomenon challenges this intuition. When students cut and rejoin, ask them to count shared edges explicitly and subtract twice that edge length from the sum of both perimeters. Watch for arithmetic errors in the L-shape and T-shape configurations where the boundary is not a simple rectangle.
materials: 6 cm × 4 cm paper chit (one per student or pair)

periods.activity_title: 9 Squares: Hunting the Smallest and Largest Perimeter

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Making it 'More' or 'Less', section 6.1 p.145
textbook_items_in_class.description: Arrange or draw different connected figures made from 9 unit squares; find the smallest and largest possible perimeters, make a figure with perimeter 18 units, and explore the effect of attaching one more unit square to a figure of perimeter 24 units.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Making it 'More' or 'Less' Q1, section 6.3 p.145
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using 9 connected unit squares, find the smallest possible perimeter.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Making it 'More' or 'Less' Q2, section 6.3 p.145
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using 9 connected unit squares, find the largest possible perimeter.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Making it 'More' or 'Less' Q3, section 6.3 p.145
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using 9 connected unit squares, make a figure with a perimeter of 18 units.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Making it 'More' or 'Less' Q4, section 6.3 p.145
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine whether other shaped figures can be made with the same perimeters found in Q1–Q3, or whether only one shape gives each perimeter; explain the reasoning.

time_bands.activity: Pose the guiding question: if area is fixed (9 unit squares), can the perimeter still change? Students predict yes or no, and briefly justify. Introduce the task from Making it 'More' or 'Less', section 6.1 p.145 ("Arrange or draw different connected figures made from 9 unit squares....") and establish the rule that squares must share at least one full side to be connected.

In pairs, students draw or cut arrangements of 9 unit squares on grid paper, computing the perimeter of each. They work through Making it 'More' or 'Less' Q1, section 6.3 p.145 ("Using 9 connected unit squares, find the smallest possible perimeter.") — the compact 3×3 square — and Making it 'More' or 'Less' Q2, section 6.3 p.145 ("Using 9 connected unit squares, find the largest possible perimeter.") — the linear 1×9 strip. Then they create a figure satisfying Making it 'More' or 'Less' Q3, section 6.3 p.145 (perimeter 18 units).

Class discussion on Making it 'More' or 'Less' Q4, section 6.3 p.145 ("Determine whether other shaped figures can be made with the same perimeters...."). Students share their arrangements and argue whether a given perimeter value can be achieved by more than one shape. Derive the rule: attaching a new square adds 2 exposed sides if one side is shared, or 4 sides if placed at a corner touching two sides.

periods.teacher_notes: The key generalisation students should reach is that shared sides reduce the perimeter, so compact arrangements (many shared sides) give smaller perimeters and linear arrangements (fewest shared sides) give larger ones. Students often miss that a diagonal attachment (corner touch) shares only one side — ask them to count exposed sides carefully. For the target perimeter of 18, multiple valid arrangements exist, and accepting several builds the idea that area alone does not determine perimeter.

periods.activity_title: Area Formulas: Rectangles, Squares, and Composite Subtraction

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (floor and carpet), section 6.2 p.137
textbook_items_in_class.description: A floor 5 m × 4 m has a square carpet of side 3 m laid on it; find the area of the floor that is not carpeted: 20 – 9 = 11 sq m.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (four flower beds), section 6.2 p.137-138
textbook_items_in_class.description: A piece of land 12 m × 10 m has four square flower beds of side 4 m at the four corners; find the area of the remaining part: 120 – 64 = 56 sq m.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.2 p.138
textbook_items_in_class.description: A rectangular garden 25 m long has area 300 sq m; find the width.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.2 p.138
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the cost of tiling a 500 m × 200 m plot at ₹8 per 100 sq m.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 6.2 p.138
textbook_items_in_class.description: A coconut grove 100 m × 50 m; each tree needs 25 sq m; find the maximum number of trees.

time_bands.activity: Begin by tiling a rectangle drawn on the board with unit squares and counting — students observe that area equals the number of unit squares that cover the region without gaps or overlaps. Build from this to the formulas: area of rectangle = l × b and area of square = s². Establish that area is measured in square units (sq m, sq cm, etc.) and that the unit square tiles a region perfectly — unlike circles, which leave gaps.

Walk through Example (floor and carpet), section 6.2 p.137 ("A floor 5 m × 4 m has a square carpet of side 3 m laid on it....") and Example (four flower beds), section 6.2 p.137-138 ("A piece of land 12 m × 10 m has four square flower beds...."). Emphasise the composite-subtraction strategy: compute the whole, then subtract the parts removed.

Students independently attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 6.2 p.138 ("A rectangular garden 25 m long has area 300 sq m; find the width."), Figure it Out Q2, section 6.2 p.138 ("Find the cost of tiling a 500 m × 200 m plot at ₹8 per 100 sq m."), and Figure it Out Q3, section 6.2 p.138 ("A coconut grove 100 m × 50 m; each tree needs 25 sq m...."). Review answers as a class.

periods.teacher_notes: A persistent error is multiplying area by the cost rate without adjusting for the 'per 100 sq m' unit in Q2 — students compute total area and multiply by 8 directly, missing the division by 100. Highlight unit conversion as a separate step. For the garden question, students who confuse area and perimeter formulas will add instead of divide; prompt them to write 'area = l × b' before substituting.

periods.activity_title: Composite Figures: Splitting L-Shapes and Frames

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4a, section 6.2 p.138
textbook_items_in_class.description: Split figure a (L-shaped composite) into rectangles and find its area in metres.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4b, section 6.2 p.138
textbook_items_in_class.description: Split figure b (rectangular frame) into rectangles and find its area in metres.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using tangram pieces, explore and identify which pieces have the same area.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine how many times bigger Shape D is compared to Shape C; describe the relationship between Shapes C, D, and E.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine which tangram shape has more area: Shape D or Shape F; give reasons.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 6.2 p.139
homework.description: Determine which tangram shape has more area: Shape F or Shape G; give reasons.

time_bands.activity: Pose the problem: how do you find the area of an L-shape or a frame that is not a simple rectangle? Model one splitting on the board, then students attempt Figure it Out Q4a, section 6.2 p.138 ("Split figure a (L-shaped composite) into rectangles....") and Figure it Out Q4b, section 6.2 p.138 ("Split figure b (rectangular frame) into rectangles...."), comparing addition of parts vs. subtraction of the inner rectangle.

Distribute or draw the tangram on paper. Students use Figure it Out Q1, section 6.2 p.139 ("Using tangram pieces, explore and identify which pieces have the same area.") to compare pieces by placing one atop another. They then use Figure it Out Q2, section 6.2 p.139 ("Determine how many times bigger Shape D is compared to Shape C....") and Figure it Out Q3, section 6.2 p.139 ("Determine which tangram shape has more area: Shape D or Shape F....") to reason about area relationships without measuring — using the structure of the tangram square.

periods.teacher_notes: For composite L-shapes, students often choose a valid split but then assign wrong dimensions to the sub-rectangles — they copy an outer dimension onto an inner piece. Encourage them to label every side length before computing. In the tangram questions, the goal is reasoning with relative areas (shape A is twice shape B), not numerical computation — watch for students who try to measure rather than reason from the tangram structure.
materials: Tangram printout or hand-drawn tangram on paper

periods.activity_title: Area vs. Perimeter: Grid Exploration and House Plans

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compare the area of Shape A to Shape G; determine whether A is twice or four times as big as G.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of the big square formed with all seven tangram pieces in terms of the area of Shape C.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Arrange the 7 tangram pieces into a rectangle and state its area in terms of Shape C; give reasons.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 6.2 p.139
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compare the perimeters of the square and the rectangle formed from the 7 tangram pieces; explain whether they are the same or different.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Let's Explore (24 sq units), section 6.2 p.141
textbook_items_in_class.description: On grid paper, make as many whole-number rectangles as possible with area 24 sq units; identify which has the greatest perimeter (a), the least perimeter (b), and explore the pattern for area 32 sq cm (c).

time_bands.activity: Students complete tangram reasoning via Figure it Out Q5, section 6.2 p.139 ("Compare the area of Shape A to Shape G...."), Figure it Out Q6, section 6.2 p.139 ("Find the area of the big square formed with all seven tangram pieces...."), Figure it Out Q7, section 6.2 p.139 ("Arrange the 7 tangram pieces into a rectangle...."), and Figure it Out Q8, section 6.2 p.139 ("Compare the perimeters of the square and the rectangle formed from the 7 tangram pieces...."). The key insight from Q8: equal-area shapes can have different perimeters.

On grid paper, students enumerate all whole-number rectangle dimensions for area 24 sq units using Let's Explore (24 sq units), section 6.2 p.141 ("On grid paper, make as many whole-number rectangles as possible with area 24 sq units...."). They compute perimeters and identify the greatest (most elongated: 1×24) and the least (most square-like: 4×6). Students conjecture which shape gives the minimum perimeter for a fixed area and test the pattern with 32 sq units.

periods.teacher_notes: The key discovery is that for a fixed area, the rectangle closest to a square minimises perimeter while the most elongated maximises it — this is a central insight that connects area to perimeter reasoning. Students may miss factor pairs (e.g., forget 3×8) — prompt them to list factor pairs of 24 systematically. For Q8, some students expect equal-area shapes to have equal perimeters; Q8 refutes this and is worth a brief class discussion.
materials: Tangram from previous unit or re-drawn

periods.activity_title: House Plans and Area Maze Puzzles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Let's Explore Q1, section 6.2 p.141
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area in square metres of the floor outside of the school corridor.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Let's Explore Q2, section 6.2 p.141
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area in square metres occupied by the school playground.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (Charan's house), section 6.2 p.146
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using Charan's house floor plan (30 ft × 35 ft overall), find the missing room dimensions and total house area.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (Sharan's house), section 6.2 p.147
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using Sharan's house floor plan (42 ft wide), find missing room dimensions and total area; compare areas and perimeters of both houses.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Area Maze Puzzles Qa, section 6.2 p.148
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given sub-rectangle areas 13, 26, and 15 sq cm in a 2×2 grid arrangement, find the missing fourth area.

homework.book_ref: Area Maze Puzzles Qb, section 6.2 p.148
homework.description: Given two sub-rectangles of 10 sq cm each with dimensions 2 cm and 3 cm visible, find the missing area of the third sub-rectangle (3 cm × 2 cm top right).

time_bands.activity: Students apply composite area to real school spaces: Let's Explore Q1, section 6.2 p.141 ("Find the area in square metres of the floor outside of the school corridor.") and Let's Explore Q2, section 6.2 p.141 ("Find the area in square metres occupied by the school playground."). They recover missing dimensions from the floor plan by working back from given totals.

Students work through the architectural problems: Figure it Out (Charan's house), section 6.2 p.146 ("Using Charan's house floor plan (30 ft × 35 ft overall), find the missing room dimensions....") and Figure it Out (Sharan's house), section 6.2 p.147 ("Using Sharan's house floor plan (42 ft wide), find missing room dimensions...."). They recover missing room dimensions by reasoning that the room widths along a side must sum to the overall dimension.

Introduce Area Maze Puzzles Qa, section 6.2 p.148 ("Given sub-rectangle areas 13, 26, and 15 sq cm in a 2×2 grid arrangement, find the missing fourth area."). Students discover that the shared side between adjacent sub-rectangles is the key to unlocking the puzzle — a multi-step chain of reasoning using area = l × b.

periods.teacher_notes: House plan problems require students to recover missing dimensions before they can compute area — this is an inverse skill that goes beyond direct formula application. Remind students to mark every recovered dimension on the plan before computing room areas. In Area Maze Puzzle Qa, students who try to find all side lengths first will become stuck; encourage guessing a shared side, using it to find adjacent areas, and checking consistency.

periods.activity_title: Area Maze: Multi-Step Reasoning with Sub-Rectangles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Area Maze Puzzles Qc, section 6.2 p.148
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given a composite figure with total height 15 cm, sub-rectangles of 42 sq cm and 60 sq cm with some dimensions given, find the missing top sub-rectangle area.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Area Maze Puzzles Qd, section 6.2 p.148
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given two stacked sub-rectangles with areas 38 sq cm and 18 sq cm and dimensions 4 cm and 5 cm visible, find the missing width (top side length) of the larger rectangle.

time_bands.activity: Return to the Area Maze strategy: from a known sub-rectangle area and one side, compute the other side. Students apply this chain to Area Maze Puzzles Qc, section 6.2 p.148 ("Given a composite figure with total height 15 cm, sub-rectangles of 42 sq cm and 60 sq cm....") where the total height provides an additional constraint that ties the sub-rectangle heights together.

Students tackle Area Maze Puzzles Qd, section 6.2 p.148 ("Given two stacked sub-rectangles with areas 38 sq cm and 18 sq cm and dimensions 4 cm and 5 cm visible, find the missing width...."). The strategy: use the 18 sq cm sub-rectangle and one known side to find the shared side, then use that shared side and 38 sq cm to find the target width.

Students create their own small area maze: draw a rectangle subdivided into two sub-rectangles, fill in two sub-areas and one side length, and exchange puzzles with a partner to solve. This reversal of the problem-posing direction consolidates the reasoning chain of area = l × b as a two-way relationship.

periods.teacher_notes: Area maze puzzles develop the idea that area = l × b works backwards: given area and one side, the other side follows by division. Students who rush to find all dimensions first will cycle without progress; encourage the chain approach — one unknown at a time. The student-created puzzle task in the last band is brief and closed: students draw, label, swap, and solve, all within the remaining minutes.

periods.activity_title: Cutting the Rectangle: Why a Triangle is Half

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Cut rectangle activity, section 6.3 p.142
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw a rectangle, draw one diagonal, cut along the diagonal to produce two triangles; check whether the triangles overlap exactly and have the same area. Repeat with rectangles of different dimensions and with a square. Use grid paper to verify the triangle-rectangle area relationship for both right triangles and non-right triangles.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 6.3 p.143
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the grid, find the area of blue triangle BAD in rectangle ABCD.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 6.3 p.143
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using the grid, find the area of red triangle ABE by decomposing into triangles AEF and BEF over sub-rectangles AFED and BFEC.

time_bands.activity: Each student draws a rectangle on grid paper, draws one diagonal, and cuts along it following Cut rectangle activity, section 6.3 p.142 ("Draw a rectangle, draw one diagonal, cut along the diagonal to produce two triangles...."). Students place one triangle atop the other and confirm they coincide exactly: the two triangles are congruent, so each has exactly half the rectangle's area. Repeat with a square and one other rectangle.

Students work Figure it Out Q1, section 6.3 p.143 ("Using the grid, find the area of blue triangle BAD in rectangle ABCD.") by counting grid squares for the whole rectangle and halving. Then tackle Figure it Out Q2, section 6.3 p.143 ("Using the grid, find the area of red triangle ABE by decomposing into triangles AEF and BEF....") — here the apex E does not sit above a base vertex, so the triangle must be decomposed into two right triangles, each half of a sub-rectangle.

Draw the general argument on the board: any triangle with base b and height h sits inside a rectangle of dimensions b × h, and the decomposition into two right triangles shows each is half its sub-rectangle. Together they give area = ½ × b × h. Students articulate the reasoning in their own words before writing the formula.

periods.teacher_notes: The critical moment is the non-right triangle in Figure it Out Q2 — students who believe the formula only applies to right triangles will resist the decomposition argument. Emphasise that the height h is perpendicular to the base, not a side, and that the apex E can be anywhere along the top of the enclosing rectangle. Watch for students who try to measure a slant side as the height.

time_bands.activity: Demonstrate one composite figure decomposition on the board: identify each sub-region (rectangle or triangle), compute each area separately, and add. Establish the strategy: enclose the figure in a rectangle if needed, compute the enclosing area, and subtract the unwanted triangular corners.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1a, section 6.3 p.144 ("Find the area of composite figure a on the grid...."), Figure it Out Q1b, section 6.3 p.144 ("Find the area of composite figure b on the grid...."), Figure it Out Q1c, section 6.3 p.144 ("Find the area of composite figure c on the grid...."), Figure it Out Q1d, section 6.3 p.144 ("Find the area of composite figure d on the grid...."), and Figure it Out Q1e, section 6.3 p.144 ("Find the area of composite figure e on the grid....") on grid paper, labelling sub-regions before computing.

Students share at least two different decomposition strategies for the same figure (e.g., addition of parts vs. enclosure-and-subtract). Class discusses: do both strategies give the same answer? Why should they? This consolidates the principle that area does not depend on the decomposition method chosen.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error is identifying the height of a triangle incorrectly — students often use the slant side instead of the perpendicular height. Encourage them to draw the height explicitly as a dotted line and count grid squares for it. For the enclosure-and-subtract approach, watch for students subtracting more corner triangles than actually exist in the figure.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 6.3 p.149 ("Give dimensions of a rectangle whose area equals the sum of the areas of a 5 m × 10 m rectangle and a 2 m × 7 m rectangle.") and Figure it Out Q2, section 6.3 p.149 ("A rectangular garden 50 m long has area 1000 sq m; find its width.") and Figure it Out Q4, section 6.3 p.149 ("Four flower beds 2 m × 1 m at corners of a garden 15 m × 12 m; find available lawn area."). These consolidate the composite-subtraction and inverse-area strategies from earlier in the chapter.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q5, section 6.3 p.149 ("Draw Shape A (area 18 sq units) and Shape B (area 20 sq units) such that Shape A has a longer perimeter than Shape B.") — a design challenge where they must deliberately elongate Shape A and make Shape B compact, drawing on the understanding that larger area does not guarantee larger perimeter.

Figure it Out Q8, section 6.3 p.149 ("A square is folded in half and cut into two rectangles; identify which of four statements (a–d) about area and perimeter relationships is always true.") is worked as a class discussion. Students use the half-area principle established through the cutting argument: the two rectangles together have the same area as the original square, but their combined perimeter is greater. Students vote on each statement and justify their choice.

periods.teacher_notes: Question 5 is an open design task — multiple valid answers exist, and students should be encouraged to share different examples. The key is that a thin elongated shape (e.g., 1×18) has a large perimeter for its area, while a compact shape (e.g., 4×5) has a smaller perimeter for a slightly larger area. Question 8 is a reasoning question: the correct statement is about area halving, while statements about perimeter halving are false — watch for students who assume perimeter scales the same way as area.

items.prompt: A rectangle has a perimeter of 18 cm and a breadth of 3 cm. What is its length?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 cm. Using P = 2 × (l + b): 18 = 2 × (l + 3), so l + 3 = 9, giving l = 6 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply P = 2 × (l + b), substitute P = 18 and b = 3, then solve for l.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student computed half the perimeter (9) and then doubled it instead of subtracting the breadth, arriving at 12.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student subtracted only the breadth once from the full perimeter (18 – 3 = 15) without halving first.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student halved the perimeter correctly (9) but forgot to subtract the breadth, giving 9 instead of 6.

inclusivity.support: Let the student write P = 2 × (l + b) and substitute the known values before solving step by step.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find a second rectangle with the same perimeter but a different length and explain how many such rectangles exist.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1a, section 6.1 p.132
exercise.description: Find missing length of a rectangle whose perimeter is 14 cm and breadth is 2 cm.

items.prompt: A wire is bent into a rectangle that is 8 cm long and 4 cm wide. The wire is then straightened and bent into a square. What is the side length of the square?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 cm. Perimeter of rectangle = 2 × (8 + 4) = 24 cm. Square side = 24 ÷ 4 = 6 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the rectangle's perimeter, then divide by 4 to get the square's side length.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student used only the breadth of the rectangle as the square's side, confusing the two shapes' dimensions.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student computed the perimeter correctly (24) but divided by 2 instead of 4, treating the square as having two pairs of sides.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student used only the length of the rectangle as the square's side, ignoring the perimeter calculation.

inclusivity.support: Prompt the student to find the total wire length (rectangle's perimeter) first, then think about sharing it equally among four equal sides.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find the side of a regular hexagon formed from the same wire and compare the two perimeter distributions.

items.prompt: A rectangular swimming pool is 30 m long and has an area of 450 sq m. What is the width of the pool?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 15 m. Area = l × b, so 450 = 30 × b, giving b = 450 ÷ 30 = 15 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Substitute into Area = l × b and divide the known area by the known length.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student subtracted the length from the area (450 – 30 = 420), treating area and length as additive quantities.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student added the length to the area (450 + 30 = 480), confusing the relationship between area and dimension.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student multiplied the area by the length (450 × 30 = 13 500), reversing the direction of the formula.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to write Area = length × width, substitute the two known values, and identify which quantity is missing before computing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to state the perimeter of the pool and then explain whether two different rectangles could have the same area but different perimeters.

items.prompt: The figure below is an L-shaped room. The outer rectangle is 10 m wide and 8 m tall. A rectangular portion 4 m wide and 3 m tall has been cut from the top-right corner. Find the total area of the L-shaped room in square metres. Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 68 sq m. Strategy 1 (subtraction): full rectangle = 10 × 8 = 80 sq m; cut portion = 4 × 3 = 12 sq m; L-shape = 80 – 12 = 68 sq m. Strategy 2 (addition): split into a 6 m × 8 m rectangle (48 sq m) and a 4 m × 5 m rectangle (20 sq m); total = 48 + 20 = 68 sq m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the area of the enclosing rectangle and subtract the cut portion, or split the L into two rectangles and add their areas.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to draw the full enclosing rectangle and then shade the cut corner; compute each area separately before combining.
inclusivity.challenge: Invite the student to find a second way to split the L-shape and verify that both decompositions give 68 sq m.

items.prompt: Priya draws a rectangle on grid paper and then draws one diagonal to form two triangles. She claims that each triangle has exactly half the area of the rectangle, and that this is true for any rectangle — not just the one she drew. Explain why Priya's claim is correct. Your explanation should describe what happens when you cut the rectangle along the diagonal and what this tells you about the areas of the two triangles.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: When the rectangle is cut along the diagonal, two triangles are produced. Placing one triangle on top of the other shows they coincide exactly — they are congruent. Because the two triangles together make up the whole rectangle and they have the same shape and size, each must have exactly half the rectangle's area. This reasoning works for any rectangle because the diagonal always splits it into two congruent triangles, regardless of the rectangle's dimensions.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Argue from the congruence of the two cut triangles: equal-area, congruent pieces each occupy half the whole.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student physically cut a rectangle along the diagonal, stack the two pieces, and describe in words what they observe before writing the explanation.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to extend the argument: if the apex of a triangle can be anywhere above the base (not just at a corner of a rectangle), does the half-area relationship still hold? How would they explain that?

items.prompt: A 10 cm × 4 cm rectangle is cut into two equal halves along its length, giving two pieces each 10 cm × 2 cm. The two pieces are joined side by side along their 10 cm edges to form a new rectangle. What is the perimeter of the new shape? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: When the two 10 cm × 2 cm pieces are joined along their 10 cm edges, the shared edge (10 cm) disappears from the boundary. The new rectangle is 10 cm × 4 cm — the same as the original — with perimeter 2 × (10 + 4) = 28 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the rejoined shape, find its outer dimensions, and apply P = 2 × (l + b).

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student sketch both pieces separately, then draw them joined, and trace the outer boundary carefully to count all exposed sides.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find a different arrangement of the same two pieces that gives a smaller perimeter, and explain why the perimeter changes.

items.prompt: Nine unit squares are arranged in a connected figure. What is the smallest possible perimeter for such a figure? Describe the arrangement that gives this minimum and explain why no arrangement of nine connected unit squares can have a smaller perimeter. Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The smallest perimeter is 12 units, achieved by the 3 × 3 square arrangement. In a 3 × 3 square, each interior shared side removes 2 units from the boundary; 12 shared sides exist (6 horizontal interior edges × 2 + 0 — but systematically: total sides = 9 × 4 = 36, shared sides = 12 pairs, each removing 2 units, so perimeter = 36 – 2 × 12 = 12). Any other connected arrangement has fewer shared sides and therefore a larger perimeter. The 3 × 3 square is as compact as possible, maximising shared sides.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count total sides of all unit squares, subtract twice the number of shared interior edges; the 3 × 3 square maximises shared edges.

inclusivity.support: Give the student squared paper and ask them to draw the 3 × 3 square and a 1 × 9 strip, count the boundary squares of each, and compare.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to investigate whether a 4 × 4 square with one corner removed (15 unit squares) gives the minimum perimeter for 15 squares, and what that perimeter would be.

items.prompt: A tangram square is made from seven pieces. Shape C is the smallest triangle in the tangram. Shape A is the largest triangle. Without measuring, explain how many times bigger Shape A is compared to Shape C, and give a reason based on the tangram's structure.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Shape A is four times the area of Shape C. The tangram square can be divided into regions whose areas are multiples of Shape C. Shape A is the large right triangle; two Shape C triangles make one Shape D (medium triangle), and two Shape D triangles make one Shape A. So Shape A = 2 × Shape D = 2 × 2 × Shape C = 4 × Shape C.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the tangram's doubling structure: D = 2C, A = 2D = 4C.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to place two Shape C pieces on top of Shape D to see that D = 2C, then repeat to compare D with A.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to express the area of the entire tangram square in terms of Shape C and verify that all seven pieces together account for that total.

items.prompt: A large rectangle is divided into two smaller rectangles by a vertical line. The left sub-rectangle has area 36 sq cm and the right sub-rectangle has area 48 sq cm. The total height of the large rectangle is 6 cm. Find the total width of the large rectangle. Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Height = 6 cm (shared by both sub-rectangles). Left width = 36 ÷ 6 = 6 cm. Right width = 48 ÷ 6 = 8 cm. Total width = 6 + 8 = 14 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide each sub-rectangle's area by the shared height to find each width, then add the two widths.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student find the width of the left sub-rectangle first using width = area ÷ height, then repeat for the right sub-rectangle.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to compute the area of the whole rectangle directly and verify that it equals 36 + 48 = 84 sq cm.

items.prompt: Two rectangles are stacked vertically. The bottom rectangle has an area of 24 sq cm and a width of 6 cm. The top rectangle has the same width as the bottom rectangle and a height of 5 cm. Find the area of the top rectangle and the total area of the combined shape. Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Bottom rectangle height = 24 ÷ 6 = 4 cm. Top rectangle: same width = 6 cm, height = 5 cm, so area = 6 × 5 = 30 sq cm. Total area = 24 + 30 = 54 sq cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the bottom rectangle's area and width to find the shared width, then compute the top rectangle's area directly.

inclusivity.support: Guide the student to find the height of the bottom rectangle first (as a separate step) and use the result to confirm the shared width before computing the top area.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find the total perimeter of the combined stacked shape using the recovered dimensions.

items.prompt: A composite figure on grid paper consists of a rectangle 6 units wide and 4 units tall, with a triangle sitting on top. The triangle's base spans the full 6-unit width of the rectangle, and its apex is 3 units above the top edge of the rectangle. Find the total area of the composite figure in square units. Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Rectangle area = 6 × 4 = 24 sq units. Triangle area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 6 × 3 = 9 sq units. Total area = 24 + 9 = 33 sq units.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute rectangle area using l × b and triangle area using ½ × b × h, then add the two regions.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to enclose the triangle in its own small rectangle (6 × 3) and take half, then add the result to the rectangle below.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to move the triangle's apex to a different position along the top edge (not the centre) and verify that the triangle's area stays the same, explaining why.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Field area = 20 × 15 = 300 sq m. Pond area = ½ × 20 × 8 = 80 sq m. Remaining area = 300 – 80 = 220 sq m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute total field area and triangle area separately, then subtract.

inclusivity.support: Prompt the student to solve in two steps: find the pond area first, then subtract from the field area.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student what would happen to the remaining area if the pond's height were doubled to 16 m, and whether the remaining area would halve.
